summary: Full text of the 2025 Hypertension meta-analysis (38 RCTs, 2,709 adults, oral magnesium 82.3-637 mg/day) shows a modest pooled BP reduction (SBP -2.81, DBP -2.05 mm Hg) with high heterogeneity, concentrated in hypertensive and hypomagnesemic participants; this matches the record's Cardiovascular/Heart Health claim and gets one eligible context. The two migraine sources (oral RCT 8792038; IV/oral meta-analysis 26752497) fall outside that claim and get no credit. A new applicability block limits credit to cardiovascular (BP) outcomes.

applicability.studied_population: Adults aged 18-77 in 38 RCTs of oral magnesium (82.3-637 mg elemental/day); BP reductions were seen in hypertensive and hypomagnesemic participants, not in normotensive participants.

identity.preparation: Elemental magnesium supplied through multiple separately named salts; not a single interchangeable preparation

population.description: 38 RCTs, 2,709 adults aged 18-77 (1,448 magnesium, 1,392 placebo; 131 in 5 crossover trials); 17 trials in hypertension (6 on BP-lowering medication, 9 untreated), 8 in normotension, 8 in hypomagnesemia (serum Mg <=0.74 mmol/L). Pregnant participants and trials altering medication or diet during the intervention were excluded.

study_contexts.study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized placebo/control-controlled trials of >=4 weeks (33 parallel, 5 crossover), with subgroup analyses, mixed-effects meta-regression and restricted-cubic-spline dose-response analysis; trials using other routes of magnesium administration were excluded at full-text review.

outcomes.name: Pooled change in systolic BP versus placebo: -2.81 mm Hg (95% CI -4.32 to -1.29), P<0.001; diastolic BP -2.05 mm Hg (-3.23 to -0.88), P<0.001; I2 78% (SBP) and 88% (DBP); 38 trials.

Hypertension subgroup SBP -2.96 (-5.53 to -0.38) and DBP -2.10 (-3.44 to -0.77); hypertensive on BP-lowering medication SBP -7.68 (-12.67 to -2.69); untreated hypertensive SBP -0.90 (-3.94 to 2.14), P=0.56; hypomagnesemia SBP -5.97 (-8.52 to -3.41); no significant change in normotensive or normomagnesemic participants.
No linear or nonlinear dose-response relationship between elemental magnesium dose and BP change (all P>=0.20).

limitations: 9 trials low bias, 25 some concern, 4 highrisk; most had incomplete randomization/concealment reporting.

Salt counts overlap conditions: chloride 7, citrate 4, oxide 8, aspartate hydrochloride 8, pidolate 4, chelate 2, lactate 4, hydroxide 2, sulphate 2, diclycine 1. Salt equivalence is not established; chloride/aspartate subgroup findings must retain their scope.
The review does not establish a universal nutrition, sleep, migraine or salt-specific effective-dose benchmark.
Primary study identifiers mapped from cited reference links: 38 cited studies, 37 Pub Med identifiers; missing identifiers not invented.

Supplement Table S 2 acquired via Europe PMC supplementary Files; exact study-specific salt, elemental dose, duration, population and background medication table retained in magnesium_supplement_tables.json. Main-body pooled ranges do not replace that table.

1 included source citations have no printed PubMed identifier in this primary source; their exact citations are retained in the source-table receipt. This is a documented identifier limitation, not a fabricated identifier or an extra independent trial.
The source designates no single primary outcome; pooled SBP/DBP change is the review's main analysis and is recorded with hierarchy not_reported rather than an invented primary label.
The main text names salt types but not the physical dosage form of each trial; dosage form is recorded as trial-specific oral preparations, not inferred.

Included reference 54 (Rylander 2004) delivered magnesium in mineral water and reference 61 (Walker 2002) was a hawthorn pilot with a magnesium arm; the review classed both as magnesium supplementation. Benefit concentrated in hypertensive participants on medication and in hypomagnesemia; untreated hypertensive and normotensive participants showed no significant SBP change. This is a modest surrogate BP effect, not cardiovascular event prevention.

population.description: 81 patients aged 18-65 with IHS-defined migraine, mean attack frequency 3.6 per month, after a 4-week prospective baseline.

study_contexts.study_design: Prospective, multicenter, placebo-controlled, double-blind randomized trial; 12-week treatment after 4-week baseline.

dose.administration_frequency: daily (abstract: 600 mg (24 mmol) magnesium daily; split schedule not reported in abstract)
dosage_forms: oral trimagnesium dicitrate (physical form not reported in the abstract)
co_therapies: Symptomatic acute-migraine medication use recorded as an outcome; no assigned co-therapy reported in the abstract.
dose.reported_regimen: Oral 600 mg (24 mmol) magnesium as trimagnesium dicitrate daily for 12 weeks, or placebo.

normalization.basis: Abstract states 600 mg (24 mmol) magnesium daily; one tested regimen, not a benchmark.

source_provenance.location: PubMed abstract (full text not open access).

outcomes.name: Attack frequency weeks 9-12 versus baseline: -41.6% magnesium versus -15.8% placebo (p<0.05).
Migraine days and symptomatic drug use per patient decreased significantly; attack duration, intensity and drug use per attack not significant. Diarrhea 18.6%, gastric irritation 4.7%.

limitations: Migraine prophylaxis is outside this record's claim (Cardiovascular/Heart Health), so this context carries no credit for the record.
Abstract only: primary-outcome designation, dosage form and split schedule are not reported there and are not inferred.
Single small 1996 trial of one salt (trimagnesium dicitrate); does not establish other salts or doses.

limitations: Chiu 2016: 21 RCTs, 11 of intravenous magnesium for acute migraine (948 participants) and 10 of oral magnesium for prophylaxis (789); oral magnesium reduced migraine frequency and intensity (ORs 0.20 and 0.27) (abstract). Not this record's cardiovascular claim; no regimen or included-study list encoded because full text was not retrieved. Not a finding that the source is invalid.
